The paper presents an approximation for modeling electromagnetic scattering from thin dielectric disks that is valid across all frequencies.
The approach involves approximating the fields inside the disk using the fields that would exist in a dielectric slab of the same thickness, orientation, and dielectric properties.
For very thin disks where T << λ, the solution reduces to an electrostatic approximation.
For disks where kA >> 1, the solution reduces to a physical optics approximation.
The solution is applicable when the dimension characteristic of the disk's cross-section (e.g. diameter) is much larger than the disk's thickness (A/T >> 1).
When the relative dielectric constant is close to 1 and kTβ << 1, the solution reduces to the Born approximation.
The radar cross section is given by σ = σ0 |Rp|^2 δpq, where σ0 is the physical optics form, Rp is the Fresnel reflection coefficient, and δpq is the Kronecker delta.
For very thin disks with A/T = 3,000, the theory showed excellent agreement with experimental radar cross section measurements, particularly near normal incidence.
For disks with A/T = 5, the theory showed reasonably good agreement with experimental data for incidence angles less than about 30 degrees.
The theory ignores edge effects, which become important when the incidence angle is greater than about 60 degrees.
The ideal experiment to fully test the theory would involve measuring scattering from a single thin disk as a function of frequency, covering the range from kA << 1 to kA >> 1.
Dielectric disks are important models for objects encountered in nature such as leaves, crops, and ice crystals in clouds.
An exact solution for scattering from a dielectric disk has not yet been found, and the paper presents an approximation that can be used across all frequencies.
The approximation has the advantage of using a solution to Maxwell's equations to represent the fields inside the disk, rather than relying on ad-hoc assumptions.
The paper compares the theoretical results to experimental data on the radar cross section of thin dielectric disks, showing good agreement in both the high and low frequency regimes.
